title: Coros Dura 2 Solar GPS First Impressions: Stay Tuned – Travis Engel
content:
The new Coros Dura 2 Solar GPS has more features, a bigger screen, and a sleeker design than the original Dura Solar, which it has now officially replaced. And its battery life is still measured in days, not hours. Travis dives into the details to answer the question: Is it worth more than twice the price?

Coros did not play it safe when it launched its first on-bike device in 2024. The Dura Solar boasted a 120-hour run time on a single charge despite a relatively small battery. And it could run even longer if it got enough sunlight. That was possible thanks in part to its MIP (memory-in-pixel) display that doesn’t refresh the whole screen when displaying motion, just the pixels that change. The thing was so frugal with its Watts that the “off” button was hidden deep within a settings sub-menu.

On top of that, it was controlled with a rotating knob, it featured a not-small-but-not-big 2.7” screen, and it cost just $250. That’s more than $200 cheaper than a Wahoo Elemnt Roam, less than half the price of a Hammerhead Karoo, and much less than half the price of a Garmin Edge 850. The original Dura Solar’s software was a little flawed at launch, but Coros released updates and added features until it earned its place in the pantheon of high-end GPS units. And the designers at Coros didn’t even have a previous model to iterate upon. There was no telling what would happen when they did.

Coros Dura 2 Solar Quick Hits

  • 3.5” screen, up from 2.7” on original Dura
  • 336 x 620 resolution, up from 240 x 400 on original Dura
  • 38hz refresh rate, faster than original Dura
  • 100g, same as original Dura
  • Memory-in-pixel display
  • Touchscreen control, plus pinch & zoom
  • Two physical side buttons, plus two haptic face buttons on solar panel
  • Optional voice control
  • Offline re-routing when connected to companion app, no cell signal required
  • Displays street and trail names, even when offline when maps are downloaded
  • IP67 waterproof rating
  • 120 hours of battery life, 70 hours in dual-frequency mode (claimed)
  • 2 hours of additional run time per 1 hour of direct sunlight (claimed)
  • $549 with alloy mount ($79 mount only, available in 25.4-31.8 clamp or 2-bolt out-front)
  • $499 (device only)
  • Available for purchase Tuesday, November 3rd

The Dura 2 Solar is what happened. And although its price point stepped right in line with the old guard of prestige devices, its package and polish leapfrogged past them. Half of the Dura 2 Solar’s 115mm X 55mm total footprint is just 5.7 mm thick. And it’s partially bordered by aluminum with a siiiick carbon fiber backplate. It’s got 63% more total screen area and significantly higher pixel density. But it still weighs almost exactly the same as the original. And most importantly, Coros is claiming the same runtime of 120 hours, or 70 hours when in the more accurate dual-frequency mode.

I’ve only been using my Dura 2 Solar for about ten days, having done several long rides at full brightness and performed a fair bit of off-bike fiddling. I’m sensing that it’s draining slightly faster than my original Dura would in the same conditions, but not meaningfully faster. I have full confidence that I could take it on a week-long tour with no hotel nights and I wouldn’t have to even ask the fine folks at Carl’s Jr. for an outlet. And if I did, the small battery (Coros is keeping the exact size a secret) charges extremely quickly. My test unit has barely lost 40% of its battery, and the power has been on non-stop aside from a number of restarts during setup. I think those restarts make for a good segue into a quick sidebar.

Stay Tuned…

A week and a half using the Coros Dura 2 Solar was the perfect amount of time for me to outline its features and offer a general critique of its feel and function. And given what a splash the original Dura made, I wanted to do it as soon as possible. But for various reasons, my experience hasn’t been the whole experience. Some of the Dura 2’s most interesting perks won’t be available until a few of its post-launch firmware updates hit. And that’s fine. This is how digital product launches sometimes work these days.

Yep, I’m making another one of my beloved video-game analogies. No Man’s Sky, a galactic exploration sim, and Cyberpunk 2077, a dystopian action RPG, saw significant improvements in the months and years after they went on sale. The Dura 2 Solar is already much more polished than either of those games were at launch. But regardless, Coros is planning a laundry list of useful updates coming in the near future. So, I decided it wouldn’t be fair for me to deliver a definitive verdict until the device itself delivers on more of its promises.

And there are a lot of them; The Dura 2 Solar will very soon allow you to have multiple custom bike profiles, enter a destination via voice control, tweak how turn-by-turn direction alerts behave, customize the function of the left physical button, pin and save your location mid-ride, and get even deeper under the hood of your training regimen. Then, the day before I handed this in, an update dropped that I haven’t had time to test, including tire-pressure-sensor support and an optimized activity-settings page.

And then there are the bugs that will be submitted and addressed as Coros responds to initial feedback on the Dura 2 Solar. First on my list is its annoying tendency (shared with the original Dura) to briefly spin the map around when I come to a stop. Coros has told me that this bug “will be fixed.” I’ve also been experiencing an odd inconsistency in receiving text, email, and other notifications on the device. The Coros tech-support team has been very responsive. They’ve walked me through a lot of troubleshooting, hence the aforementioned restarts and fiddling.

That’s why I added the nebulous phrase “First Impressions” to this review title. We’re discouraged from using it unless we plan on returning to update a review. And I do plan to. But for now, I definitely can judge some things. So, let’s get into it.

Buttons

The first-generation Dura’s rotating knob was polarizing, to say the least. Probably a smart move to ditch it for the second gen. The Dura 2’s generously textured side buttons protrude drastically. Even through gloves, you know your fingers are in the right place. And those buttons require a firm press. I never started, stopped, or paused a ride accidentally. The right button is essentially an “enter” button. The left is “back” or “cancel,” and a long press will enter voice-control mode.

The haptic ↑ and ↓ face buttons effectively take the place of the original Dura’s knob. The haptic function is off by default, but I recommend turning it on. The simulated tactility trained me to use the correct amount of pressure. These buttons are “resistive,” not “capacitive,” meaning they respond to force, not flesh. They work great with gloves and don’t get the least bit confused in the rain. I might have preferred traditional buttons, but their current design allows them to double as the solar panel.

Overall, it’s an intuitive, familiar layout that’s persisted since the days of Cateye and Avocet. You can access and navigate most features using only physical buttons. The face buttons scroll between data pages, while the side buttons are more for entering and exiting menus and activities. But that does leave a few tasks to the touchscreen.

Touchscreen

Scrolling is not quite as smooth as a smartphone, displaying a very slight visual stutter. But it’s close. It’s as good as I’ve seen from an on-bike device. And mine almost never ignores a single-point tap, especially without gloves. Single taps, by the way, are how I selected my activity type before starting a ride. It’s the only technically mandatory touchscreen operation, but it’ll likely happen in a controlled environment.

When not in a controlled environment, the screen’s wet-weather performance is perfectly average. You can’t fight physics, and even a benign mist will eventually collect into droplets. I’d have to wipe it dry before I could tap or swipe again. But the only phantom action I witnessed was an occasional unwanted ringing of the new bike-bell function, normally actuated with a double tap.

The performance gap between the Dura 2 and a smartphone becomes a bit more noticeable when you use its touchscreen to manipulate the map. The visual stutter is slightly more drastic when moving around more data in more dimensions. And it occasionally took an instant for the map’s incoming edge to load if I swiped too far or too fast, though I’ll admit that was when I was intentionally trying to push its limits. So, this is totally fine within the scope of a GPS’s specific duties. And tapping the map screen’s + and – buttons is a quick, reliable way to zoom in and out.

Display

It’s impressive that Coros increased the screen size without significantly increasing the device footprint. That certainly allows the map page to provide more information, and pairs well with the improved street- and trail-name integration. But until Coros fixes the compass-spinning bug, that map page is literally disorienting when I’m not in motion. And when I am in motion, I’m mainly just following a bright blue line of breadcrumbs. The original Dura did that fine.

Complex tasks like changing plans or researching points of interest have always been better handled on a phone anyway. But I’d prefer to leave my phone in my pocket whenever possible. Once the compass bug is fixed, I have high hopes that the Dura 2’s bigger, higher-definition screen will eventually allow it to handle frequent tasks like checking if a shortcut goes through or ensuring I should take that sharp right and not that really sharp right.

I actually found the larger screen had the most impact when viewing ride data. It offers ample real estate to see elapsed time, time of day, distance, elevation gain, elevation loss, and even an elevation profile all on one page. That’s really all the information I needed. I don’t have a power meter, and my heart couldn’t maintain its target beats-per-minute even if I had Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero to guide it. But for the biometrics nerds out there, the Dura 2’s big color screen really gives those ever-fluctuating graphs and numbers room to breathe.

The MIP screen’s brightness and vibrance still doesn’t match those of an AMOLED display like you’d find on a smartphone. But I can’t point to a moment when that bothered me on a ride. By design, the information displayed by our on-bike devices is simple. Sure, the Dura 2’s reds and oranges may look a little similar when you suddenly pass out of even shade into harsh sunlight. But our brains are wired to help fill in those gaps. As long as I had the brightness at 50% or higher, I never struggled to make meaning of what the device had to tell me. It’s not a 3D Super Mario game. That minor cosmetic compromise is worth the major increase in battery life.

Voice Control

I always feel a little silly when talking to a machine. I avoid it when I can, especially in public. My limited experiences using voice control on the Dura 2 did not change my mind. When I once told it to “set backlight level to maximum,” the screen displayed the response, “command not supported.” But when I said “set brightness level to maximum,” I was met with, “backlight set to 100%.” At least the thing has a sense of humor.

I had a hard time thinking of functions I’d use the voice control for. The Dura 2 can monitor my AXS drivetrain battery life, which would be nice to access via voice because I don’t need it to be on my data screen for an entire ride. But either that can’t be accessed via voice command, or I didn’t use the right words. One category of functions that would be easier to control by voice is training. You can tell the Dura 2 to alert you when you cross the threshold into a specific heart rate or power zone, neither of which are settings you’d need always at your fingertips.

And then there’s the voice-activated navigation function Coros is working on adding in the future. I’ve had great success using the original Dura to navigate me to places I choose on the Coros app. Since voice control requires the phone to be paired, I assume most of the phone-based navigation functions will be accessible through it. When I’m in a city I don’t know, I’d love to hold a button and say, “Take me to Carl’s Jr.” Unless I’m east of the Mississippi, where I’ll have to remember to say “Hardee’s.”

 

Accessory Integration

Not much is changing in terms of wireless accessory integration aside from the addition of tire-pressure sensors, but I wanted to touch upon it. You can easily pair biometric sensors and even various radar-alert rear lights. But I’m most interested in how it integrates wireless bike components, and I think it could use some refinement on that front. I have multiple SRAM AXS components spread across two bikes, but as of now, there’s no way to collect any of them under a single bike’s umbrella.

For those who do want a constant reminder of their wireless drivetrain’s battery life, it’d be nice for their gravel-bike activity profile to include data fields for their gravel bike’s drivetrain. That may be a feature available in the upcoming update allowing for custom bike profiles, but we’ll have to wait and see. As for wireless dropper post battery life, Coros tells me that likely isn’t possible. I had to use my SRAM AXS phone app to check my Reverb battery, which already groups it together with my drivetrain battery. So in my case, it wouldn’t be worth bothering to involve the Dura 2 in checking either.

App Functionality

Speaking of apps, the Coros companion app stays the same. But it’s worth a brief visit. Even without voice help, the in-app map and navigation function is pretty impressive. As long as it has a data connection, you can search for businesses and intersections just as intuitively as you would on Google Maps. And making a custom route has all the basic functions you may already be used to, plus a freehand “erase” feature that’s more precise than the undo button.

The app can still orchestrate a head-spinning number of training functions, but again, I’m unfortunately not qualified to evaluate them. Coros’s head start in the fitness wearables space naturally gives it an edge in this category, so the app will have everything you’d expect. But Coros still managed to add a little more.

Other New Features

Coros offers a number of “workouts” that guide you during a ride, jumping back and forth between heart-rate and/or power zones. Those workouts can now be started and paused mid-ride. There’s also an improved FTP testing function, and a couple new power metrics available as data-page items. But again, I’m not the one to critique training utilities. I’d rather listen to podcasts.

While the original Coros eventually added media control as an optional data cell, the Dura 2 accesses a media-control screen via a left swipe. It can pause, adjust volume, skip music tracks, or skip forward a few seconds in a podcast. I’d love to be able to scroll through my downloaded episodes, but maybe that’s asking too much.

There are also a handful of other tweaks. There’s that digital bike-bell sound I mentioned, which is impressively loud and surprisingly convincing. I’d prefer to map it to the left button, but that’ll have to wait for an update. And even offline, the Dura 2 has a remarkably accurate database of street and trail names that are visible when zooming in on the map, or in turn-by-turn directions. You can now edit the data fields directly on the device; you can add pinned locations to your library for easy navigation to your favorite spots from wherever you happen to be; and supposedly, you can get climb notifications even when you’re not following a saved route. Despite multiple attempts, though, I never got that feature to work. Really, the update I’m most stoked about is offline re-routing.

Offline Re-routing

There’s not much to say about this feature other than “it works.” Or more accurately, “it works really well.” Previously, the best you’d get was a dotted line pointing at the nearest segment of your route, which may be over a mountain. Now, it does real-time recalculating if I go off course. Even in the middle of nowhere. For as long as is reasonable, it would direct me to turn around and get back in line. But at the appropriate moment, it would pick a modified path towards the nearest intersection on my original route. The trail names would update, as would the distances to intersections. It works really well.

All you need to do is download the map for your region to both your phone and to the device, both of which are totally free and very thorough. But they take up surprisingly little data. The devices Coros sent to the media had literally the entire globe saved to them, and they still had 2 gigabytes of the 32-gigabyte storage left over. And I have all of Southern California downloaded to my phone, and it takes up less than 100 megabytes.

Construction and Mounting

The Dura 2 can be purchased with or without a handlebar mount. Now that Garmin-style mounts are as ubiquitous as USB-C cables (which the Dura 2 does come with), you probably already have a mount you like. Plus, the slim and sleek alloy mount may be a little too slim and sleek for some. I don’t like its 2.5mm hex-head bolt. I prefer the 3mm bolts used in the plastic Garmin-style mounts I had on hand. And there’s a techy locking mechanism to help prevent theft, but I once accidentally activated it after removing the device during a late-ride grocery run (can’t be too careful with unreleased products). I didn’t bring the included SIM card removal pin required to disengage it, so I rode the rest of the way home with the device in my pocket.

*Quick side note: We weren’t sure who would have time to review the Dura 2, so Mara here at The Radavist got a test sample as well. And the night before I handed in this review, she also accidentally engaged the locking mechanism with the device uninstalled. It made me feel seen.

The structure of the device itself is more impressive than the mount. The aluminum frame might seem unnecessary, but the stronger, thinner materials likely bought Coros some precious cubic millimeters when maximizing space for the screen, processors, and battery. Plus, the aggressively stepped profile actually makes it quite ergonomic to hold when off the bike. And on the bike, it concentrates most of its mass just above the mounting interface. It’s the definition of “refined.” Although I think vibes should never be a primary concern in product design, I’ll admit I really like the Dura 2’s vibes.

Value

Let me start this section by saying clearly that I like the Dura 2 more than the original Dura. It offers a meaningfully better user experience. And as the updates roll in, it will get better still. Although Coros is now boutique buddies with Wahoo, Hammerhead, and Garmin, its mastery of battery life puts it well beyond the stagnant status quo. For me, GPS units are most crucial on multi-day rides. The Dura 2 Solar is the only one that actually lasts multiple days. It is the one to buy. But until we see a few more updates, I say that with acceptance, not excitement.

If the original Dura had remained in the lineup as-is for $250, I believe that model would still be the one to buy. It had all the most valuable features of the Dura 2 for less than half the price. When I first learned the original Dura would be discontinued, I wondered if the sudden AI-driven boom in tech-hardware pricing might have made its low price impossible in 2026. I asked Coros CEO Lewis Wu whether that’s been a factor, and while he said GPS units aren’t immune to that trend, they’re not getting hit as hard as things like graphics processors and solid-state drives. “The cost tends to be a marginal difference per unit,” Wu says. “And it hasn’t driven up our pricing across any products directly.”

Photo: Coros

Wu tells me the shift to a higher-end focus was just Coros giving the people what they want. “We identified a clear demand among consumers for a premium bike computer that matches the quality and aesthetics of their high-end bikes,” Wu explains. “[The Dura 2 Solar’s] pricing reflects the investment we’ve made in premium materials, engineering, and design.”

Photo: Coros

I guess I can’t argue with that. Such a fundamental redesign just two years into a product’s run is an expensive endeavor. Plus, keeping the original Dura in the lineup would come with costs of its own. It would take up production bandwidth and add market confusion. Personally, though, I think it’d be a bit like Toyota discontinuing the Land Cruiser and only offering the Lexus GX. But what do I know? I’ve got a base-level 2006 Tacoma.

If this ship has sailed, and GPS manufacturers are prioritizing the luxury market, I think we should start expecting more from them. You can get a lot of technology for $500. Like a Nintendo Switch 2 after its recent price increase. Or like my third-generation iPhone SE. It isn’t made anymore, but it cost $450 when it was released in 2022 and $150 on the refurbished market today. Yet, the list of things my iPhone can do that the Dura 2 can’t is miles longer than what the Dura 2 can do that my iPhone can’t.

I asked Wu about this as well. I’m not an engineer or an economist, so I’m sure there’s something I’m missing here. “While you can get all the cycling data you want on your phone, there isn’t a single app that optimizes it all for use while cycling the way a cycling-specific computer does,” Wu tells me. “We weigh every feature against battery drain to make sure cyclists are getting the functionality they need without impacting the battery life our customers expect.” He has some points there. It was probably vital to keep the Dura 2 Solar’s list of capabilities lean to avoid too many sub-programs fighting for battery life. And a phone app called Cadence can track and display data, but it doesn’t integrate navigation and routing. It also requires a paid subscription. Wu points out, Coros “does not and will not” charge extra for software functions.

Maybe I’m being impatient. Offering smartphone-like features on third-party devices is clearly a complex process. The first dashboard screen I ever used was in a rental car with only a janky native navigation app and no brightness adjustability. My parents’ late-model luxury sedan now allows me to port Google Maps along with all the preferences saved to my phone, though the pairing process is often a comedy of errors. It’ll take time, but I trust that progress will come. In fact, as I’m writing this, Garmin just updated its 1060 model to include voice-controlled navigation. But it costs $800.

Presumably, Coros intends this hardware update to stick around for a while. So, there may be lots of time to add features that we haven’t even considered. I’m optimistic that I’ll speak of it with a more glowing tone when I come back to this. And while I’m being optimistic, Coros played it coy when asked about a lower-priced device someday entering the lineup. I hope that happens. The 2006 Tacoma crowd is staying tuned.

Pros:

  • Maintains its class-leading battery life by a wide margin
  • Modestly sized device
  • Luxuriously sized screen
  • Simple, familiar interface
  • Touchscreen use not required
  • Excellent offline re-routing
  • High-quality free downloadable maps
  • Deep training functionality
  • Useful in-app route planning
  • Convenient pinned destinations
  • Future updates hold almost limitless promise

Cons:

  • It needs those future updates soon
